name: Dibothriocephalus latus

taxonomy.rank_note: Reference groups can include multiple species. Protozoan higher-rank systems differ; the lineage is provided without forcing every clade into a class rank.

morphology: Egg: approximately 55–75 × 40–50 µm, yellow-brown and operculated, sometimes with a small opposite-end knob; unembryonated when passed.
Broad proglottids may have a central rosette-shaped uterus.

transmission.detail: Aquatic stages pass through a copepod and fish; humans acquire plerocercoids in raw or undercooked fish.

life_cycle.detail: Aquatic stages pass through a copepod and fish; humans acquire plerocercoids in raw or undercooked fish.
Operculated eggs and proglottids in stool.

hosts: Definitive: humans and fish-eating mammals. Intermediate: copepod then fish; larger fish may be transport hosts.
distribution: Mainly temperate freshwater regions; imported fish and travel make fish tapeworms relevant to Thai laboratories.
clinical_significance: Often mild gastrointestinal illness; some infections are associated with vitamin B12 depletion and megaloblastic anemia.
specimen: Operculated eggs and proglottids in stool.
diagnostics: Wet mounts at 100–400×; molecular testing can resolve related fish tapeworm species.
differential_diagnosis: Egg morphology alone does not securely distinguish related diphyllobothriid species; avoid equating every fish tapeworm with D. latus.
review_status: Source-compiled educational content; not independently clinically validated

annotation_guidance: Record specimen, stage, stain, objective/total magnification, pixel calibration, source image and reviewer certainty.
Native crops of 200–650 pixels do not determine biological size. Retain µm-per-pixel calibration before resizing.
Split training, validation and test data by patient/specimen; keep related crops in the same split.
Keep damaged or ambiguous objects uncertain. Molecular confirmation of a mixed specimen does not assign every pictured object a species.
